content: The user is typically responsible for constructing the toilet and pit, although they may hire a mason to perform the work. The user is also responsible for cleaning and maintaining the toilet, including the slab, seat or squat hole, drop-hole, cover or lid, and the superstructure. To minimize odors and insect breeding, a cup of soil, ash, or sawdust should be added to the pit after each defecation. Periodically adding leaves can improve the pit's porosity. When the pit becomes full, the user must dig a new pit, transfer the toilet and superstructure to the new location, and cover and fill the old pit. If desired, a tree can be planted on top of the old pit. Maintenance for a closed pit is minimal, aside from caring for any tree planted on the abandoned pit. Trees planted in such pits require regular watering and protection from animals, which can be achieved by constructing a small fence around the sapling. The toilet separates users from excreta, while the pit isolates excreta and pathogens from physical human contact. During rainfall, the toilet and pit contain fresh excreta, preventing it from being washed into surface water bodies. Users do not come into contact with fecal material, significantly reducing the risk of pathogen transmission. Pathogen reduction occurs primarily through extended storage time in the pit. The conditions within the pit are unfavorable for pathogen survival, leading to their die-off over time, typically within one to two years. This process can be accelerated by adding lime or other alkaline materials to raise the pH, increasing the temperature, or reducing the moisture content. Ascaris (roundworm) eggs are the most persistent pathogens to die off. Any leachate from the pit safely permeates into the surrounding soil, where pathogens are filtered out, adsorbed onto soil particles, or die off during their slow movement through the soil. A dry toilet system, such as a urine-diverting dry toilet (UDDT), is designed to produce a solid, earth-like material using alternating pits or a composting chamber. Inputs to the system may include urine, feces, organics, cleansing water, and dry cleaning materials. The system does not use flush water, and water should not be introduced into it. The dry toilet is directly connected to a double ventilated improved pit (double VIP), fossa alterna, or a composting chamber for containment. Alternating containers allow the material to degrade and transform into pit humus, a nutrient-rich, hygienically improved material safe for excavation. When one pit is full, it is covered and allowed to rest for at least two years while the other pit is in use. This cycle can be repeated indefinitely. Properly operated composting chambers can also produce safe, usable compost. The twin-pit pour-flush system is a water-based system that uses a pour-flush toilet (squat pan or pedestal) and twin pits to produce a partially digested, humus-like product. Inputs include feces, urine, flush water, cleansing water, dry cleaning materials, and greywater. The twin pits are lined with porous material, allowing liquid to infiltrate the ground while solids accumulate and degrade at the bottom. When one pit is full, it is covered and allowed to rest for at least two years while the other pit is in use. After resting, the contents transform into pit humus, which is nutrient-rich and safe for use as a soil conditioner or disposal. The emptied pit is then put back into operation, and the cycle can be repeated indefinitely. The success of these systems depends on proper operation and extended storage periods. The decomposition process is enhanced if a continuous source of soil, ash, or organics (e.g., leaves, grass clippings, coconut or rice husks, wood chips) is available. The required storage time can be minimized if the material remains well-aerated and not overly moist. Workers handling the material during removal, transport, and end use must wear appropriate personal protective equipment. The toilet should be constructed from materials such as concrete, fiberglass, porcelain, or stainless steel for ease of cleaning and to prevent stormwater infiltration. For pit-based technologies, the water level and groundwater use must be considered to avoid contaminating drinking water. Pits should be installed in areas located downgradient of drinking water sources and at a minimum horizontal distance of 15 meters. Non-degradable solid waste removed from the container must be properly disposed of, either through regulated solid waste management services or burial. The pit humus or compost produced is generally safe to handle and can be used as a soil conditioner in agriculture. If there are concerns about pathogen levels or the quality of the material, it can undergo further composting in a dedicated facility before use. If no end use is identified, the treatment product can be permanently disposed of.
